utterance_src: چه قابل دارد؟ از خود شماست، ببرید.
context: Speaker: carpet seller, about fifty, in a city bazaar. Listener: a first-time customer who has just agreed a price for a small rug. The customer takes out money and the seller waves it away with this phrase.
literal_render: What worth does it have? It's yours — just take it.
intent_render: Please, don't mention it — you're most welcome. (Ritual waiver: payment at the agreed price is still fully expected; the customer should insist.)
pragmatic_note: A buyer who takes the waiver literally and walks out without paying has, in the seller's eyes, stolen the rug.
phenomenon: taarof: ritual refusal of payment (qabel nadara)

utterance_src: نه تشکر، زحمت نکشید، همین حالا چای خوردم.
context: Speaker: a wholesale buyer visiting a supplier's office for the first time this season. Listener: the supplier, who has just offered tea. This is the buyer's response to the first offer.
literal_render: No thanks, don't trouble yourself, I just had tea.
intent_render: Oh, please don't go to any trouble. (A ritual first refusal: the host is expected to insist, and the guest will then accept.)
pragmatic_note: If the host's side reads the refusal as final and cancels the tea, the meeting starts cold and the buyer feels slighted.
phenomenon: taarof: ritual first refusal and re-offer of hospitality

utterance_src: این حرف‌ها چیست؟ میان ما پول جای ندارد.
context: Speaker: an uncle who lent money to his nephew's shop. Listener: the nephew, who has just tried to hand back the first repayment at a family gathering. They work in the same bazaar.
literal_render: What is this talk? Money has no place between us.
intent_render: Come now, no need for that between family. (Ritual refusal: the nephew must insist two or three times; the repayment is still owed and expected.)
pragmatic_note: If the nephew takes the refusal at face value and stops repaying, the debt silently poisons the family relationship.
phenomenon: taarof: ritual refusal of repayment among kin

utterance_src: وظیفه‌ام بود، پول نمی‌گیرم.
context: Speaker: a young porter who carried a merchant's goods across the bazaar. Listener: the merchant, holding out a tip. The porter pushes the money back with this phrase.
literal_render: It was my duty, I won't take money.
intent_render: It was nothing, really — I couldn't. (Ritual refusal of a tip: the merchant should press it into his hand once or twice more, and he will accept.)
pragmatic_note: A foreign reader who pockets the tip after one refusal shortchanges a worker who was being polite, not declining income.
phenomenon: taarof: ritual refusal of payment for service

utterance_src: کار ما قابل شما نیست، یک چیز ناچیز است؛ امید که بد نشده باشد.
context: Speaker: a tailor delivering a finished wedding suit he is proud of. Listener: the groom's father, a long-time customer, opening the package in the shop.
literal_render: Our work is not worthy of you, it is a trifling thing; I hope it hasn't turned out badly.
intent_render: I hope it pleases you — we did our best for you. (Formulaic self-deprecation: the tailor is proudly presenting good work and inviting a compliment, not admitting defects.)
pragmatic_note: Read literally, the maker appears to confess poor quality, and the customer may reject the goods or demand a discount.
phenomenon: self-deprecation not to be believed (shekasteh-nafsi)

utterance_src: اختیار دارید، هر چه شما بگویید.
context: Speaker: a fabric seller mid-bargain. Listener: a regular customer who has just named a low price. The seller says this while folding the fabric, clearly not yet agreeing.
literal_render: You have the authority — whatever you say.
intent_render: You're too kind — but let's be fair to us both. (Deference formula in bargaining: it concedes face, not the price; a fair counteroffer is still expected.)
pragmatic_note: Read literally the seller has accepted any price the customer names, which inverts an ongoing negotiation into a closed deal.
phenomenon: bargaining politeness: deference formula (ekhtiar darid)
draft_flag: Check whether 'اختیار دارید' alone reads Iranian; Dari speakers may prefer 'صاحب‌اختیار هستید'.

utterance_src: ان‌شاءالله ببینیم خدا چه می‌خواهد؛ خبرتان می‌کنیم.
context: Speaker: a dried-fruit supplier who cannot fill a large rush order. Listener: a new export buyer pressing for double the usual volume before the holidays. Spoken at the end of the meeting.
literal_render: God willing, let us see what God wants; we will inform you.
intent_render: We'll see — I wouldn't count on it. (A polite, face-saving refusal: no commitment is being made and none should be planned for.)
pragmatic_note: If the buyer books shipping against this 'we will inform you', the soft no becomes a supply-chain failure.
phenomenon: indirect refusal via inshallah-deferral

utterance_src: فکرهایم را می‌کنم، باز خدمت می‌رسم.
context: Speaker: a customer at the door of a gemstone shop after an hour of viewing. Listener: the shopkeeper, who has offered his final price. The customer leaves with this phrase.
literal_render: I will do my thinking and will come to your service again.
intent_render: Let me think it over — thank you for your time. (Polite exit: this is almost always a final no; the shopkeeper should not hold the stone.)
pragmatic_note: A seller who reserves the goods on the strength of this phrase loses other buyers waiting on a customer who is not coming back.
phenomenon: indirect refusal: polite exit formula
draft_flag: Dari naturalness of 'فکرهایم را می‌کنم' — Iranian would be 'فکرهامو می‌کنم'; confirm register.

utterance_src: باشد، ببینیم چه می‌شود.
context: Speaker: a shop owner responding to his cousin's proposal to invest in expanding the shop. Listener: the cousin, who has laid out the plan over dinner. The owner has doubts he will not state openly at the table.
literal_render: Okay, let's see what happens.
intent_render: We'll see. (Non-committal deferral functioning as a soft refusal: the cousin should read this as reluctance, not as agreement in principle.)
pragmatic_note: The English 'okay' makes it sound like consent, so the cousin may start spending against a partnership that was never agreed.
phenomenon: indirect refusal: bashad-deferral among kin

utterance_src: به خدا شرمنده‌ام، رویم سیاه است؛ تا آخر هفته پول‌تان را می‌رسانم.
context: Speaker: a shopkeeper behind on payment to his wholesaler of ten years. Listener: the wholesaler, who has come in person to ask about the balance. Spoken quietly at the back of the shop.
literal_render: By God I am ashamed, my face is black; I will deliver your money by the end of the week.
intent_render: I'm deeply sorry — I've failed you on this, and you'll have your money by the end of the week. (The shame formula signals the promise is binding and the relationship matters.)
pragmatic_note: Literal 'my face is black' reads bizarre or worse in English, and dropping the shame formula strips the promise of its binding weight.
phenomenon: obligation framing: ritualized shame before a creditor (ru-siyahi)

utterance_src: دست شما درد نکند، ما نمک‌گیر شما شدیم.
context: Speaker: a trader whose partner covered a customs fee for him without being asked. Listener: that partner, on the phone the next day. They have traded together for three years.
literal_render: May your hand not hurt; we have become caught by your salt.
intent_render: Thank you — truly, we're in your debt now. (The salt idiom creates a standing obligation of loyalty and reciprocity, not a casual thanks.)
pragmatic_note: If the obligation dimension is deleted, the partner's later expectation of reciprocity looks like it comes from nowhere.
phenomenon: obligation framing: namak-gir (bound by salt)

utterance_src: بنده در خدمتم؛ هر امری داشته باشید، دریغ نمی‌کنم.
context: Speaker: a mid-level supplier closing a deal with a larger distributor. Listener: the distributor's owner, older and better established. Spoken while shaking hands at the end of the meeting.
literal_render: Your servant is at your service; whatever order you have, I will not withhold.
intent_render: It's been a pleasure — anything you need, don't hesitate. (Formal self-lowering courtesy: goodwill and availability, not servitude or an open-ended commitment.)
pragmatic_note: Rendered literally it reads obsequious or like a contractual blank check, distorting a standard courtesy between unequal partners.
phenomenon: obligation framing: self-lowering service formula (bande dar khedmatam)

utterance_src: کاکا جان، هر چه شما صلاح می‌بینید؛ فقط اگر اجازه باشد، یک عرض کوچک داشتم.
context: Speaker: the youngest partner in a family import business. Listener: his father's elder brother, who has just decided to take a large loan for the business. The others at the table have said nothing.
literal_render: Dear uncle, whatever you see fit; only, if permitted, I had one small petition.
intent_render: Uncle, of course it's your decision — but with respect, I have serious concerns I need to raise. (Maximal deference packaging a real objection; the 'small petition' is anything but small.)
pragmatic_note: If the deference is read literally, a substantive objection to a risky loan disappears into politeness.
phenomenon: deference to elders: objection wrapped in petition formula (arz)
draft_flag: کاکا is Dari (paternal uncle); Iranian Farsi would be عمو — item is Dari-register by design.

utterance_src: شما بزرگ ما هستید، اختیار با شماست.
context: Speaker: a shopkeeper in a dispute with a neighboring shopkeeper over a shared storeroom, addressing the elder trader both sides asked to mediate. Spoken in front of the other party.
literal_render: You are our elder; the authority is with you.
intent_render: We respect you and will hear your judgment. (Ceremonial deference to a mediator: it grants face and a hearing, not unconditional surrender of the claim.)
pragmatic_note: Read literally it converts a courtesy owed to a mediator into a binding waiver of the speaker's position.
phenomenon: deference to elders in dispute mediation

utterance_src: Hi Ahmad — just a reminder that the invoice is now two weeks overdue. Please arrange payment by Friday.
context: Speaker: a young export manager writing from abroad. Listener: an elder Afghan wholesaler, a partner of eight years who has always eventually paid. The manager wants payment without damaging the relationship.
literal_render: سلام احمد — فقط یادآوری می‌کنم که بل حالا دو هفته ناوقت شده است. لطفاً پرداخت را تا روز جمعه ترتیب کنید.
intent_render: سلام و احترامات خدمت شما احمد آقا. ببخشید که مزاحم می‌شوم؛ اگر زحمت نباشد، حساب آن بل را که دو هفته پیش موعدش گذشته، تا جمعه یک ترتیبی بفرمایید. ممنون شما هستیم.
pragmatic_note: The blunt rendering reads as a public accusation of bad faith to an elder; the firm-but-honorific version gets paid without burning eight years of trust.
phenomenon: register: dunning an elder partner without face loss
draft_flag: Check my Dari renders for naturalness (بل for invoice, ناوقت) — please correct wording at Gate A.

utterance_src: We should definitely grab tea sometime!
context: Speaker: an American buyer wrapping up a first trade-show conversation. Listener: an Afghan rug exporter. The American means it as a friendly goodbye, not a concrete plan.
literal_render: حتماً باید یک وقتی با هم چای بخوریم!
intent_render: از آشنایی با شما خوش شدم؛ امید است باز صحبت شویم. (تعارف خداحافظی امریکایی است، دعوت جدی نیست.)
pragmatic_note: Rendered literally it lands as a real invitation, and the exporter may wait for a tea that was never planned — American ritual politeness inverted into commitment.
phenomenon: reverse taarof: American ritual invitation read literally
draft_flag: Intent render includes a parenthetical gloss; decide at Gate A whether glosses are allowed in reference renders.

utterance_src: Let me think it over and I'll circle back to you next week.
context: Speaker: a European distributor who has decided against an Afghan saffron supplier's offer but avoids saying no directly. Listener: the supplier, who invested weeks preparing samples. Written at the end of an email.
literal_render: بگذارید فکرهایم را بکنم و هفتهٔ آینده دوباره با شما تماس می‌گیرم.
intent_render: راستش را بخواهید، فعلاً برای ما مقدور نیست؛ اگر وضع تغییر کرد، خودم خدمت‌تان تماس می‌گیرم. (جواب نرمِ رد است، نه وعدهٔ جدی پیگیری.)
pragmatic_note: The literal render carries a promise of follow-up the writer never intended, so the supplier holds stock and waits for a call that will not come.
phenomenon: Western soft-no ('circle back') rendered as commitment
draft_flag: Debatable whether the intent render should make the refusal this explicit — flagging for your call.

utterance_src: Thanks so much for sorting out the shipment — we owe you one!
context: Speaker: a British importer whose Afghan partner spent a day fixing a customs problem for him. Listener: that partner. Sent as a quick text message.
literal_render: خیلی تشکر که محموله را حل کردید — یکی برای‌تان قرضدار شدیم!
intent_render: دست شما درد نکند، واقعاً زحمت کشیدید؛ این لطف‌تان را فراموش نمی‌کنیم و امید که جبران کنیم.
pragmatic_note: The casual register undersells a real favor and the literal 'owe you one' reads like an odd money debt; the gratitude-and-reciprocity formula is what maintains the partnership.
phenomenon: gratitude/obligation formula required where English is casual

utterance_src: Unfortunately we're going to have to pass on this offer.
context: Speaker: a procurement lead at a foreign firm rejecting a bid. Listener: an Afghan supplier, older than the writer, who mobilized family connections to prepare the bid. First line of an email.
literal_render: متأسفانه مجبور هستیم از این پیشنهاد بگذریم.
intent_render: از زحمات و پیشنهاد خوب‌تان صمیمانه تشکر می‌کنیم. این بار شرایط ما اجازه نداد و امیدواریم در فرصت دیگری افتخار همکاری با شما را داشته باشیم.
pragmatic_note: A bare refusal to an elder who spent social capital reads as disrespect; the softened render refuses just as clearly while returning face.
phenomenon: face-preserving refusal expected in Persian business register

utterance_src: That's very kind of you, but I really can't accept this — company policy doesn't allow gifts.
context: Speaker: a foreign inspector offered a box of saffron by a factory owner at the end of a site visit. Listener: the owner, for whom the gift is hospitality, not a bribe. The refusal is real and final, not politeness.
literal_render: خیلی لطف دارید، اما واقعاً نمی‌توانم قبول کنم — مقررات شرکت اجازهٔ هدیه را نمی‌دهد.
intent_render: لطف و مهمان‌نوازی شما را از صمیم قلب قدردانی می‌کنم، اما به راستی معذورم؛ مقررات شرکت ما به هیچ صورت اجازهٔ گرفتن هدیه را نمی‌دهد. این را تعارف نگیرید، عذر من واقعی است.
pragmatic_note: A polite-sounding refusal is heard as the ritual first 'no', so the owner will insist and re-gift; the translation must mark the refusal as genuinely final without insult.
phenomenon: real refusal that must not be heard as taarof
draft_flag: The added sentence 'این را تعارف نگیرید' is an interpretive addition — flagging for your judgment.
